titleStmt.title: Computational Auto-Archaeology: A Multi-Scale Analysis of the Language-Aesthetics Dialectic

dhq:bio.p: Dr. Fotini Mastroianni holds a PhD in Economics and Business Administration from the University of Patras (Department of Tourism Management). Her research spans two main lines: women's entrepreneurship and social reproduction — addressed in her forthcoming monograph "Pragmatic Resilience and Heritage in Women's Artisan Entrepreneurship: Gold Threads" (Palgrave Macmillan, forthcoming 2026) — and disability and workplace rights law, addressed in her forthcoming monograph "Refused and Retaliated: Disability, Workplace Rights and Institutional Failure in Greece" (Lived Places Publishing, forthcoming 2027). Her work also extends to computational approaches to cultural and philosophical discourse. In 2026 she received the Best Scientific Paper Award at the 12th International Scientific Conference of I.A.K.E. (Heraklion, Crete) for "Digital Tools as Cultural Bridges: Language, Aesthetics, and Women's Entrepreneurship in Creative Industries."

docTitle.titlePart: Computational Auto-Archaeology: A Multi-Scale Analysis of the Language-Aesthetics Dialectic

Disclosure statement: The author reports there are no competing interests to declare.

Data availability statement: The analytical configurations (Voyant Tools parameters) are detailed in Appendix A.3. The three reported correlation coefficients are presented as illustrative pattern-level observations rather than as part of a complete correlation matrix; see Appendix A.2 and A.3 for details. The blog corpus analyzed cannot be shared during blind review to maintain anonymity but will be made available upon publication with author identification.

div.head: Purpose
div.p: Contemporary aesthetic theory faces a methodological challenge: how to move beyond purely hermeneutic interpretation with anonymity but philosophical depth. This article introduces and applies computational auto-archaeology as a methodological response, demonstrating how digital text analysis can identify patterns consistent with conceptual structures operating beneath conscious philosophical argumentation.

div.head: Design/Methodology/Approach
div.p: The method treats the philosopher's own corpus as an archaeological site, using Voyant Tools for multi-scale analysis. The study employs two corpora: a developmental corpus of 25 Greek philosophical blog posts (2015–2025, 20,822 words) and a focused corpus of three essays (3,332 words) explicitly engaging language, aesthetics, and social change. Analysis combines Pearson correlations on term frequencies, chi-square tests for collocations (p<0.001), network visualization of term associations, followed by iterative qualitative interpretation.. The dual-scale design tests pattern consistency across different granularities, strengthening claims that identified associations reflect stable discourse-internal structures rather than artifacts of a single text or analytical scale.

div.head: Findings
div.p: Quantitative analysis identifies three correlations: violence with culture (r=0.73), language with resistance (r=0.68), and aesthetics with power (r=0.61), all p<0.001. This asymmetry suggests that within the analyzed discourse, aesthetics is more strongly associated with power than with resistance, while language functions as resistance's primary conceptual weapon. Network visualization is compatible with this pattern, showing aesthetics mediating between language and political transformation. These discourse-internal patterns do not claim external psychological validity but provide empirical illustration of how theoretical frameworks structure philosophical writing.

div.head: Originality/Value
div.p: The article makes both methodological and theoretical contributions. Methodologically, computational auto-archaeology extends distant reading to philosophical self-analysis, offering a complementary approach to traditional hermeneutics. Theoretically, the findings provide discourse-level illustration of Jacques Rancière's "distribution of the sensible," revealing how aesthetic-political frameworks manifest in actual philosophical discourse. The method addresses urgent questions about algorithmic governance and aesthetic power in digital culture.
Keywords: computational aesthetics, auto-archaeology, digital humanities, methodology, Jacques Rancière, Michel Foucault, aesthetic politics, distribution of the sensible

div.head: 1. Introduction: The Methodological Challenge in Aesthetic Theory
div.p: Contemporary aesthetic theory faces a methodological limitation: while hermeneutic close reading excels at interpretive depth by revealing meanings, tracing influences, and constructing philosophical arguments, it cannot expose the structural patterns that organize aesthetic discourse beneath the level of explicit argumentation. The philosopher who analyzes only consciously stated claims risks overlooking conceptual associations that operate without deliberate intention. This limitation is not merely technical but epistemological.

As Foucault demonstrated in his archaeological examination of discourse, the most significant rules governing thought and practice often function beneath the level of conscious awareness (Foucault, 1972) A discourse's explicit statements rest upon implicit foundations invisible to its participants. If this holds for historical formations, why not for philosophical reflection itself? What structural architectures organize aesthetic theory?

This article introduces and applies computational auto-archaeology as a methodological response to this question. "Auto archaeological" does not imply narcissistic self-reference but an epistemological necessity: by analyzing one's own corpus, one accesses the gradual emergence of concepts and argumentative patterns through sustained engagement with aesthetic and cultural problems. The "computational" dimension provides mediated objectivity — an algorithmic reading that identifies statistical associations and co-occurrence patterns with mathematical precision. However, this objectivity is 'mediated' rather than transcendent: algorithms encode specific assumptions and operational choices, as critical digital humanities scholarship has shown (Bucher, 2018). The patterns identified here are thus constrained by Voyant's built-in lemmatization, window-size parameters, and frequency thresholds, and should be read as algorithmically conditioned observations rather than unmediated facts.

This approach addresses a focused research question: Can digital text analysis illustrate discourse-internal architectures in the language-aesthetics relationship? The article employs multi-scale analysis: a developmental corpus of 25 Greek texts (2015–2025, 20,822 words, 530,000+ views) and a focused corpus of three Greek essays (3,332 words) explicitly engaging language, aesthetics, and social change. This dual scale tests pattern consistency across different granularities.

Findings converge on a dialectical structure. The developmental corpus reveals significant correlations: violence with culture (r=0.73), language with resistance (r=0.68), and aesthetics with power (r=0.61), all p<0.001. These discourse-internal patterns suggest an asymmetry where aesthetics is more strongly associated with power than with resistance. The focused corpus confirms this through network visualizations of term collocations (Mastroianni, 2025). These patterns remain internal to the analyzed corpus and do not claim external psychological or universal validity. They offer discourse-level evidence that resonates with Jacques Rancière's theory of the "distribution of the sensible" — the contested field determining what can be perceived and therefore politically contested (Rancière,2004). Where Rancière provides a theoretical argument, this computational analysis illustrates how such a framework can structure actual philosophical discourse. Similarly, it highlights a dimension of Michel Foucault's analysis of discourse as a power mechanism that Foucault himself did not fully develop: the role of pre-reflective affective operations in shaping the conditions of possibility for political contestation (Foucault,1972).

div.head: 2. Philosophical Foundations: Why Auto-Archaeological Analysis?
div.p: This section establishes the philosophical foundations for computational auto-archaeology. It addresses three interconnected questions: Why analyze one's own texts? How does digital analysis create objectifying distance that mitigates self-referential bias? What theoretical commitments guide the method's application to aesthetic-political discourse? Readers primarily interested in empirical findings and their theoretical implications may proceed directly to Section 3 (methodology) and Section 4 (findings).

div.head: 2.1. The Hermeneutic Circle and Its Discontents
div.p: Analyzing one's own corpus invites the charge of narcissism or circularity. However, the method's epistemic value lies precisely in its reflexivity: it examines not what an author consciously intended, but what algorithmic analysis reveals about the conceptual structures organizing their discourse. This transforms the researcher from sovereign interpreter into an archaeological subject, someone whose patterns of thought become empirically investigable rather than hermeneutically privileged.

What appears as self-reference functions epistemologically as self-estrangement. Computational auto-archaeology addresses the limitations of traditional hermeneutic reading by introducing an external perspective — not a transcendent objectivity, but an algorithmic reading that identifies statistical patterns without reference to meaning or intention. When analysis shows that "aesthetics" and "power" co-occur significantly more frequently than chance predicts (r=0.61, p<0.001), this indicates a discourse-internal conceptual association that structured thinking beneath explicit argumentation. The author did not deliberately theorize this pairing; it emerged through sustained engagement with cultural phenomena and became visible only through computational detection. The algorithm remains indifferent to authorial intentions or theoretical commitments, providing pattern-level illustrations on subsequent philosophical interpretation. This approach resonates with Franco Moretti's "distant reading," which demonstrates how computational analysis identifies patterns invisible to close reading (Moretti, 2013). Computational auto-archaeology performs similar analysis on one's own philosophical corpus. While sharing distant reading's commitment to macro-patterns, computational auto-archaeology extends this tradition in three key respects.

First, it applies computational methods reflexively to philosophical discourse rather than literary corpora (Bode, 2018; Piper, 2018). Second, it responds to critiques of interpretive significance in computational literary studies (Da, 2019) by leveraging authorial contextual knowledge to validate patterns and resources unavailable when analyzing external corpora. Third, it engages contemporary text-analysis tools that integrate natural language processing capabilities absent in earlier distant reading approaches (Manovich, 2020). This situates auto-archaeology within the broader evolution from macro-analysis to cultural analytics and AI-assisted hermeneutics.

div.head: 2.2. The Discursive Archive of Philosophy
div.p: Michel Foucault's archaeological method provides the primary theoretical grounding: discourse is governed by implicit rules that determine what can be said and thought within a given formation (Foucault, 1972) These rules operate beneath conscious awareness, structuring knowledge without being explicitly theorized by participants.

Computational auto-archaeology extends this insight by treating the philosopher's corpus as an "archive" whose implicit rules can be partially excavated through statistical pattern detection. The Violence-Culture correlation (r=0.73, p<0.001) exemplifies this. The author did not consciously theorize culture as a system producing symbolic violence, yet computational analysis shows consistent association between these concepts, resonating with Bourdieu's framework without having been deliberately invoked (Bourdieu, 1977). Such patterns remain discourse-internal: they indicate structural organization within the corpus rather than psychological repression or universal truth. The term "preconscious" here refers not to psychoanalytic repression but to associations operating beneath explicit thematic articulation.

Computational analysis identifies statistical linkages that shaped discourse without conscious theorization. These findings do not claim psychological validity; rather, they provide discourse-level evidence that resonates with theoretical examinations of pre-reflective affective operations (Ahmed, 2010; Massumi, 2002). Several methodological safeguards mitigate epistemic risks. First, algorithmic analysis produces patterns independent of researcher expectations. Second, multi-scale validation reduces selective interpretation. Third, statistical measures (Pearson correlations, chi-square tests) provide verifiable evidence that conceptual pairings reflect systematic structure rather than subjective impression.

div.head: 2.3. The "Auto-" as Epistemological Necessity
div.p: Three epistemological reasons justify analyzing one's own corpus.

First, only self-analysis grants access to the living development of concepts. The blog format created a public laboratory where ideas evolved through real-time engagement, revealing gradual emergence of theoretical structures.

Second, computational processing introduces mediated objectivity. As with any algorithmic method, however, this mediation is not neutral. The analysis reflects Voyant's own lemmatization and thresholding choices rather than a view from nowhere (Bucher, 2018). The algorithm identifies associations without philosophical agenda, often contradicting conscious self-understanding.
Third, this approach enacts a hermeneutic circle at the level of philosophical practice itself, transforming the philosopher into both subject and analyst (Heidegger, 1962).

The corpus's approximately 535,000 total views (as of January 2026) indicate notable cultural resonance for philosophical essays in Greek. In a national context where internet users number around 8.7 million (Kemp, 2025) and specialized philosophical content typically reaches limited audiences, this readership suggests that the blog format facilitated broader public engagement with theoretical discourse. However, findings remain specific to this author, context (Greece during and post-economic crisis), medium (blog), and theoretical tradition (post-Rancièrean aesthetics). The method reveals how concepts organize this particular discourse, not universal laws of aesthetic theorizing.

div.head: 2.4. Uncovering, Not Proving: A Complementary Methodology
div.p: Computational analysis must not be misconstrued as positivist reduction. The method neither replaces philosophical interpretation with statistical correlation nor substitutes quantitative measurement for qualitative understanding. Rather, it offers a complementary approach, shifting emphasis from "proving" pre-existing theories to "uncovering" latent structures within discourse itself. The relationship resembles phenomenological description and hermeneutic interpretation in Heidegger (1962). Computational analysis identifies patterns; philosophical judgment constructs meaning from them. The distinction between "uncovering" and "proving" is crucial. The method uncovers discourse-internal patterns consistent with Rancière's framework, providing illustrative evidence at the level of philosophical writing while avoiding positivist overreach. Importantly, this does not independently validate Rancière's theory: patterns may reflect prior influence rather than external confirmation.

div.head: 3. The Method: Multi-Scale Computational Auto-Archaeology
div.p: Michel Foucault's The Archaeology of Knowledge provides the primary conceptual foundation (Foucault, 1972). Foucault treats discourse not as an expression of ideas but as a practice governed by implicit rules that determine what can be said, thought, and contested within a given formation. Archaeological analysis seeks to identify these rules — the "archive" structuring knowledge without participants' full awareness. Computational auto-archaeology extends this approach by treating the philosopher's own corpus as an archaeological site: an "archive" whose implicit conceptual rules can be partially uncovered through statistical pattern detection. A multi-scale design tested pattern consistency across different levels of granularity, strengthening claims that identified associations reflect stable discourse-internal structures rather than artifacts of a single text or scale.

div.head: 3.1. Scale 1: The Focused Corpus (3 Essays)
div.p: Three Greek essays (3,332 words total) were selected using principles of theoretical sampling (Charmaz, 2014): conceptual density (highest frequency of key terms), theoretical representativeness (capturing different phases of argumentation), and contrasting structure (including both hegemonic and resistant deployments of concepts).

div.head: 3.2. Scale 2: The Developmental Corpus (25 Essays)
div.p: The larger corpus comprises 25 Greek-language blog posts (2015–2025, 20,822 words total) addressing diverse phenomena ranging from political movements to algorithmic governance and cultural critique. Consistency of patterns across these varied contexts supports claims of robust conceptual architecture rather than topic-specific clustering. The texts document a decade of theoretical development in real-time public writing.

div.head: 3.3. Analytical Technique and Visualization
div.p: Analysis employed Voyant Tools, a widely used platform in digital humanities scholarship (Sinclair & Rockwell, 2016). Terms were automatically lemmatized using Voyant's built-in algorithms to handle morphological variations (e.g., "aesthetics" and "aesthetic" unified under "aesthetic"). Collocation analysis used a five-word window (two words before and after the target term), with statistical significance assessed via chi-square tests (p<0.001). Correlation coefficients were calculated using Pearson's r on raw term frequencies across documents. Pearson's r measures the linear relationship between two variables — here, the frequency with which two terms appear across documents — ranging from -1 (perfect negative association) to +1 (perfect positive association). The p-value indicates the probability that such a correlation would occur by chance. Values below 0.001 suggest the pattern is unlikely to be random. The approach combined frequency analysis, collocation mapping, and network visualization. All reported correlations achieved statistical significance (p<0.001). From the focused corpus, two visualizations proved particularly illuminating (detailed analysis published elsewhere (Mastroianni, 2025) summarized here for relevance).

The force-directed network graph maps significant collocates within the five-word window. Aesthetics (αισθητική) emerges as the central node, mediating connections between language (γλώσσα) and revolution (επανάσταση). Edge thickness represents collocation strength. The mediated structure — language connected to revolution primarily through aesthetics — indicates a discourse-internal pattern warranting further theoretical interpretation.

The network structure is theoretically significant. Instead of direct connection between language and revolution, aesthetics mediates language connects to aesthetics, which connects to revolution. Linguistic practice achieves political efficacy through aesthetic transformation — the thesis of "creative disobedience."

Figure 2 reveals the dynamic distribution of structural terms across document segments, exposing the temporal rhythm of the argumentative structure. [See Figure 2: Word Distribution] The analysis tracks the relative occurrence of key grammatical and conceptual markers throughout the text, divided into ten equal segments. An intriguing inverse pattern emerges between the article η (“the”, feminine gender — purple line) and the particle να (“to”, subjunctive marker — green line), suggesting a rhythmic alternation between declarative and directive modes of discourse.

This pattern is philosophically significant. The article η marks declarative statements while να marks prescriptive statements. The inverse relationship shows texts oscillate between analysis and prescription, with structured zones where analysis generates prescription.
The analysis highlights zones of conceptual intensity and transitional passages. The rhythm itself enacts the dialectic it describes.

div.head: 3.4. From Patterns to Theory: Grounded Theory Methodology
div.p: Computational analysis produces empirical patterns; theoretical meaning emerges through systematic interpretation. The study followed an iterative interpretive procedure inspired by qualitative research traditions to ensure interpretations remain grounded in the data rather than imposed externally (Charmaz, 2014; Corbin & Strauss,2008). The process proceeded in three stages:

list.item: Initial pattern identification: Initial identification of recurrent statistical associations and visual patterns.
Relational categorization: Organization of patterns into relational categories (e.g., aesthetics as mediator).
Framework construction: Construction of an overarching interpretive framework from the most robust patterns.

div.p: This iterative methodology prevents confirmation bias and ensures that theoretical claims arise from discourse-internal evidence rather than preconceived frameworks. The resulting interpretation — while informed by existing theory (Rancière, Foucault) — remains anchored in the specific patterns uncovered in the present corpora.

div.head: 4. Findings: The Language-Aesthetics Dialectic
div.p: This multiscalar analysis demonstrated a consistent and robust dialectical architecture. The large-corpus quantitative data provided the broad structure; small-corpus analysis and visualisations provided the granular confirmation and illustration. The strong convergence of the findings across these two scales, despite variation in corpus size, language, and level of formality, suggests that the patterns represent genuine conceptual architecture rather than being an artefact of any one corpus or particular analytical method.

div.head: 4.1. The Three Foundational Correlations
div.p: Correlation analysis used Voyant Tools' Pearson correlation function on the 25-document corpus. The three strongest correlations:
The analysis of the 25-text developmental corpus revealed three statistically significant correlations that form the foundation of the dialectical architecture:

Violence ↔ Culture (r=0.73, p<0.001): This strong correlation suggests culture was conceptualized as a mechanism producing symbolic violence, consistent with Bourdieu's theory. The high coefficient indicates a persistent conceptual pattern across diverse contexts.

Language ↔ Resistance (r=0.68, p<0.001): This correlation suggests linguistic practice — argumentation, critique, new vocabularies — was theorized as resistance's primary weapon, consistent with Habermas. The pattern suggests a gap in aesthetic resistance theorization.
Aesthetics ↔ Power (r=0.61, p<0.001): This finding indicates aesthetics was theorized in relation to power rather than resistance. The asymmetry invites theoretical interpretation (section 4.2).

These three patterns suggest a dialectical architecture with aesthetics as the contested mediating term. The correlational evidence is consistent with a model where culture generates symbolic violence, power deploys aesthetics to naturalize this violence, and resistance employs language to denaturalize and critique it. But this linear model appears insufficient, as the focused corpus analysis suggests.

div.head: 4.2. The Dual-Level Operation: Rational-Conscious vs. Affective-Preconscious
div.p: The correlational patterns suggest that language and aesthetics function as different "weapons" operating at different levels of consciousness, providing a framework in which asymmetries may be understood. The relationship between them is dialectical in the Hegelian sense: they mutually constitute each other through reciprocal interaction-neither reducible to the other, yet each needing the other for full political effectiveness. This is not Marxian dialectic, or contradiction resolving in synthesis, but post-Hegelian dialectic, or mutual determination through ongoing interplay that never resolves into final synthesis..

The corpus patterns suggest that language is associated with the rational-conscious level through persuasion, rhetoric, and argumentation. Linguistic practice is positioned within the discourse as deliberate conscious resistance requiring awareness and rational commitment. This links with critical theory from the Frankfurt School to Habermas (Horkheimer & Adorno,2002). Resistance through language requires recognition of domination, articulation of alternatives, and arguing their validity

Aesthetics is associated in the corpus with the affective-preconscious level, characterized as influencing through desire, aversion, and sensory experience. The discourse positions aesthetic phenomena as experienced immediately, before articulation. This theorized immediacy is what gives aesthetics its political power within the analyzed framework. This connects to affect theory, which emphasizes how bodies are moved by affective atmospheres operating beneath conscious awareness (Ahmed, 2010).

This dual-level operation may explain the correlational asymmetry observed in the corpus. The discourse patterns suggest that power is associated primarily with the preconscious level through aesthetic mediation, while resistance is associated primarily with the conscious level through linguistic critique. However, effective resistance often deploys aesthetic strategies, hip-hop's sonic power precedes its political message, just as power mobilizes conscious discourse. The model describes a continuum with dominant tendencies, not a rigid dichotomy.

A terminological clarification: This analysis focuses on aesthetics as discourse — the language used to discuss beauty, form, sensory experience, and cultural value — rather than aesthetic experience itself or specific aesthetic objects. The claim is not that aesthetic philosophy or art criticism operates preconsciously, but that aesthetic discourse provides the conceptual vocabulary through which preconscious operations (what appears natural, beautiful, desirable, or normal) become available for conscious contestation and reconfiguration. Aesthetic discourse names and theorizes what power seeks to naturalize. This focus on discourse level is consistent with Foucault's archaeological method and enables computational text analysis of the conceptual structures organizing aesthetic-political thought.

This framework constitutes what might be termed the Model of Aesthetic Dispute: a theoretical architecture revealing aesthetics as the contested terrain where power's preconscious operations encounter resistance's conscious linguistic interventions. The model demonstrates that effective political transformation requires engagement at both levels — aesthetic reconfiguration alongside linguistic critique — explaining why resistance strategies limited to either dimension alone often prove insufficient.

Resistance, conversely, must work consciously through language to expose these preconscious operations, making visible what aesthetic governance renders invisible. This explains why language correlates more strongly with resistance — linguistic practice functions as the primary weapon for conscious political struggle. Language names what aesthetics naturalizes, making domination visible as domination rather than as natural order.

Yet the corpus analysis suggests that effective resistance cannot remain purely linguistic. As one text articulates: "The most powerful weapon is 'creative disobedience,' which consists in rejecting the language that seeks to be imposed and producing numerous works, particularly literary works, in the national language." Here, "creative disobedience" embodies the dialectical synthesis: conscious linguistic refusal (operating at the rational level) transforms into aesthetic creation (operating at the affective level), producing new cultural forms that reshape preconscious experience.

The corpus analysis suggests that resistance achieves full effectiveness when linguistic exposure generates new aesthetic propositions — when conscious critique becomes embodied in new forms of sensory experience, new distributions of the sensible. This dialectical movement from conscious linguistic critique to preconscious aesthetic transformation may constitute a mechanism through which political change becomes possible.

div.head: 4.3. Concrete Examples and Rhythmic Organization
div.p: While these patterns emerge from the analyzed corpus, they resonate with observable phenomena in contemporary culture. The following examples illustrate how the language-aesthetics dialectic might operate in concrete political and cultural contexts, though these applications extend beyond the corpus and would require independent empirical validation.

Cooperation: Political Advertising exemplifies cooperative deployment. Barack Obama's 2008 "Hope" campaign combined explicit policy messaging with Shepard Fairey's iconic poster — its upward gaze, patriotic color scheme, and graphic simplicity operating preconsciously. Research suggests aesthetic factors often determine response more powerfully than policy positions, with Todorov et al. finding facial appearance alone predicts election outcomes (Todorov et al.,2005).

Opposition: The Punk Movement exemplifies the oppositional relationship. The punk movement of the 1970s deployed nihilistic slogans and provocative linguistic content (language) in direct contradiction to dominant aesthetic norms, generating a new, deliberately "ugly" aesthetic of torn clothing, aggressive sound, and confrontational performance (Hebdige, 1979). Here, linguistic refusal of dominant culture transformed into aesthetic revolution — creating new forms of beauty precisely through rejection of established aesthetic standards. The movement illustrates how resistance begins with conscious linguistic rejection ("No Future") but achieves cultural impact only through aesthetic transformation (the punk aesthetic that reshaped youth culture globally).

Synthesis: Hip-Hop Culture most clearly embodies the dialectical synthesis. Hip-hop culture created new vocabularies, new forms of linguistic play, and new rhetorical strategies (language) hand in glove with new sounds, new styles of dress and movement, and new ways of occupying urban space (aesthetics) (Rose,1994). Neither dimension moved independently — the linguistic innovations (rap's complex wordplay, the invention of new slang) needed aesthetic embodiment (the sound of rap, the style of hip-hop fashion) to gain cultural power, while the aesthetic innovations needed linguistic articulation to achieve political consciousness. Hip-hop's cultural and political punch lies precisely in this synthesis of conscious linguistic creativity with preconscious aesthetic transformation.

These examples are consistent with the corpus analysis findings: effective political and cultural transformation may require both weapons operating dialectically. Language alone remains abstract, failing to reshape lived experience; aesthetics alone remains unconscious, failing to achieve critical awareness. The dialectical interplay-conscious linguistic critique generating new aesthetic practices, new aesthetic experiences requiring linguistic articulation-constitutes the mechanism through which the distribution of the sensible transforms.

The focused corpus analysis yielded a "rhythmic organization of argumentative structure" as pictured in Figure 2. The inverse relationship between declarative discourse modes, marked by the article η, "the", and the directive discourse modes, marked by the subjunctive particle να, "to", suggests a constant oscillation within the text between analysis and prescription, between describing what is and demanding what should be. This pattern is based on the relative frequency of two grammatical markers across ten segments of a 3,332-word corpus and should be read as a suggestive stylistic observation rather than a statistically validated finding. As such, this rhythmic quality is the stylistic trace of the language-aesthetics dialectic itself, which moves the argument between conscious analysis, declarative mode, and affective call to action, directive mode. It enacts at the level of discourse what it argues at the level of content: the necessity of moving between rational critique and aesthetic transformation.

div.head: 5. Philosophical Implications: Extending Aesthetic Theory
div.p: A methodological note on terminology: While Foucault's archaeology explicitly rejects Hegelian dialectics and Rancière's aesthetics resists teleological synthesis, this analysis employs "dialectic" in a post-Hegelian sense. By 'post-Hegelian dialectic' I mean a relationship of mutual constitution and persistent tension that does not resolve into synthesis — a usage distinct from Marxist dialectics of contradiction and resolution.

The language-aesthetics "dialectic" refers to their irreducible tension — each delimits and enables the other without synthesizing into higher unity. The Model of Aesthetic Dispute captures this: aesthetics functions as permanently contested terrain between power's preconscious operations and resistance's conscious interventions, not as dialectical resolution toward consensus or synthesis.

This terminological choice is philosophically necessary rather than merely rhetorical. The language-aesthetics relationship cannot be adequately captured by terms like "interaction," "correlation," or "relationship" because these suggest external contact between independent entities. "Dialectic" (understood non-teleologically) captures three essential features the data reveal: (1) mutual constitution — each term's meaning depends on its opposition to the other; (2) productive tension — the relationship generates new conceptual possibilities rather than remaining static; (3) irreducible antagonism — the tension cannot be resolved into synthesis or harmony. Alternative terms would domesticate what the computational analysis shows to be a fundamentally agonistic structure. The term's philosophical precision outweighs its potential for misreading, particularly when explicitly defined as post-Hegelian.

div.head: 5.1. Discourse-Level Illustration of Rancière's Distribution of the Sensible
div.p: The findings provide a discourse-level illustration of Jacques Rancière's theory of the partage du sensible (Rancière, 2004). For Rancière, politics is fundamentally aesthetic: it concerns struggle over what is visible, audible, and sayable. Politics happens when those rendered invisible make themselves seen and heard, disrupting the established distribution through aesthetic means.

A methodological caveat requires emphasis: Rancière's work has likely influenced the corpus analyzed here. Finding Rancièrean patterns shows how his framework organizes this discourse, not independent validation of his theory. This clarifies what auto-archaeology can show: how theoretical frameworks manifest in practice, not whether those frameworks accurately describe reality or constitute independent empirical confirmation.

With this caveat in mind, the findings illustrate how Rancière's framework operates at the discourse level. The Power↔Aesthetics correlation (r=0.61) within the corpus is consistent with the hypothesis that the existing distribution of the sensible is maintained primarily through aesthetic means: by shaping what appears beautiful, natural, or desirable, power determines what can be perceived and therefore what can be contested. The Language↔Resistance correlation (r=0.68) suggests that contestation of this distribution operates primarily through linguistic means: by naming what power renders invisible, by articulating alternative distributions, by arguing for their validity.

The model offers a potential extension of Rancière's theory by suggesting one way how the distribution might be contested: power may work primarily through preconscious aesthetic imposition, while resistance may work through conscious linguistic exposure that eventually generates counter-aesthetic practices. This specification addresses a possible limitation in Rancière's work: while he theorizes the distribution of the sensible as the terrain of political contestation, he does not fully specify the mechanisms through which this contestation unfolds. The dual-level model developed here provides this specification.

Moreover, the model explains why aesthetic politics is so difficult. If power operates at the preconscious level while resistance operates at the conscious level, resistance always faces an asymmetry: it must make conscious what power keeps preconscious. This is why "creative disobedience”, the dialectical synthesis of linguistic critique and aesthetic creation — is necessary: only by generating new aesthetic experiences can resistance operate at the same preconscious level where power maintains its grip.

div.head: 5.2. The Preconscious Dimension of Foucault's Discourse Analysis
div.p: The model provides one possible extension of Michel Foucault's analysis of discourse as a power mechanism (Foucault, 1994b). While Foucault emphasizes how language is used as a weapon, the present model points to aesthetics as an equally important weapon acting at a preconscious level. Aesthetic power shapes the conditions of possibility for discourse through determining what can be felt and perceived.

As established above (Section 5), this analysis treats the language-aesthetics relation as dialectical rather than merely correlational. Foucault's discourse analysis offers a parallel case for this same dynamic within a single domain of power.

Consider for instance Foucault's analysis of the clinic in The Birth of the Clinic (Foucault, 1994b). Here Foucault shows how medical discourse constituted the modern body as an object of knowledge. But this discursive constitution is arguably dependent upon prior aesthetic constitution: the clinical gaze rendering the body visible in specific ways, hospital architecture making certain bodies visible and others invisible, sensory training teaching doctors to see, hear, and touch bodies clinically. These aesthetic dimensions operated beneath explicit discourse, shaping what could be said by first shaping what could be perceived.

The patterns here suggest that Foucault's archaeological method could be extended to analyze not just discursive formations but aesthetic formations: the historically specific ways of seeing, hearing, and feeling that make certain discourses possible. This "aesthetic archaeology" would complement Foucault's discourse analysis by revealing the preconscious, affective foundations upon which discourse may rest.

div.head: 5.3. Temporal Acceleration in Digital Culture
div.p: The significance of this dialectical mechanism becomes evident in contemporary digital culture, where algorithmic systems mediate both linguistic and aesthetic experience. Algorithmic governance operates through linguistic constraints (hashtags, content moderation, platform-specific vocabularies) and aesthetic shaping (interface design, recommendation algorithms, infinite scroll). The corpus patterns — where aesthetics associates more strongly with power — resonate with analyses of how platforms curate visibility and shape user experience (Foucault, 1994a).

Users often experience platform interfaces as natural or intuitive. Established studies of platform design suggest that this perceived naturalness results from interfaces operating at a pre-reflective level, guiding behavior through affective cues rather than explicit commands (Bucher, 2018). The "like" button, for instance, does not command approval-seeking but structures affective experience such that it becomes habitual. These interpretations extend beyond the present corpus, drawing on existing research rather than claiming direct empirical generalization from the analyzed texts. Digital resistance responds with counter-languages (coded communication, neologisms) and counter-aesthetics (glitch art, vaporwave, dark patterns) (Russell, 2020). The corpus asymmetry — stronger aesthetic-power linkage — resonates with the observation that platforms shape experience at a pre-reflective level while resistance often begins at the conscious linguistic level. Only when resistance produces new aesthetic practices can it engage algorithmic governance on comparable terrain. While the corpus provides discourse-level illustration of this dialectic, broader claims about algorithmic aesthetics require validation through analysis of platform-specific corpora or user-experience data. The present findings suggest avenues for such future investigation.

div.head: 6. Methodological Contributions, Limitations, and Future Directions
div.p: Beyond its specific contributions to aesthetic theory, this study demonstrates the viability of computational auto-archaeology as a philosophical approach with broader applications.

div.head: 6.1. Methodological Contributions
div.p: This method offers several advantages: identifying patterns invisible to traditional close reading, providing empirical grounding through correlation coefficients, demonstrating robustness through multi-scale convergence, and suggesting cross-linguistic applicability for global aesthetic theory.

The method could be applied to analyze canonical philosophers' theoretical development, track conceptual evolution within philosophical schools, or facilitate collaborative research. Comparative studies could analyze how different aesthetic theorists conceptualize aesthetics-politics relationships, revealing similarities and differences invisible to traditional comparison. Longitudinal studies could track how philosophical vocabularies evolve over decades.

div.head: 6.2. Limitations and Constraints
div.p: The patterns identified here require validation beyond the author's corpus. The developmental corpus (25 blog posts, 20,822 words) is relatively small and stylistically homogeneous, consisting entirely of the author's own writings on aesthetic and political topics. While adequate for exploratory analysis and pattern identification, such a limited corpus cannot substantiate comprehensive claims about philosophical discourse generally. The goal here is not to characterize all aesthetic theory, but to test whether patterns identified in focused analysis (three essays) remain consistent across a larger, thematically diverse sample from the same author's work. The findings' generalizability requires validation through: (1) comparison with other philosophers' corpora to assess author-specificity, (2) analysis of larger multi-author corpora to verify cross-author consistency, and (3) examination of corpora in other languages to test cultural-linguistic variation. The present study establishes computational auto-archaeology's viability and identifies patterns warranting such broader investigation. Additionally, the Pearson correlations reported in Appendix A.2 were calculated on raw term frequencies. Without normalization for document length, these coefficients may reflect corpus-specific artifacts rather than stable conceptual relationships. Established approaches such as TF-IDF weighting or relative-frequency normalization address this document-length confound (Manning, Raghavan and Schütze, 2008), and the general pitfalls of comparing raw word frequencies across corpora of differing size are well documented in corpus linguistics (Kilgarriff, 2001). Future work should apply such normalization to validate the patterns reported here.

A basic limitation must be emphasized: this approach theorizes discourse about aesthetics, not aesthetic experience itself. Computational auto-archaeology brings into sharp focus how philosophers theorize about aesthetics, the conceptual architectures that organize aesthetic discourse, but not the phenomenology of aesthetic experience itself. This is epistemology of aesthetics, not phenomenology of aesthetic experience.

But what does the analysis of aesthetic discourse tell us about how aesthetics functions in theoretical practice? It can tell us how aesthetic concepts function in theoretical practice, how they relate to other concepts (power, resistance, language), and what implicit theories organize aesthetic thinking. To ground claims about aesthetic experience computationally, however, would require at least one more interpretive step. The correlation in philosophical discourse between aesthetics and power does not by itself prove that aesthetic experience functions as a mechanism of power; it shows that philosophers theorize aesthetic experience this way.

This is particularly pointed in the case of analyzing one's own corpus. Auto-archaeology can show how frameworks organize discourse, what architectures emerge, and which patterns persist-not whether patterns exist independently of influencing frameworks or whether they describe aesthetic phenomena accurately. It provides illustration at the level of discourse, not independent validation of claims concerning aesthetic experience.

div.head: 6.3. Future Directions
div.p: However, these limitations also constitute important indications with respect to the most promising future applications of the method. The same computational archaeological approach could be extended to:

Historical philosophical corpora: Does Kant's corpus show unconscious patterns of organization among the three Critiques? Does the interrelation among Critique of Pure Reason, Critique of Practical Reason, and Critique of Judgment exhibit patterns invisible to traditional reading? Does Rancière's own discourse present the asymmetries his theory describes? This would constitute a test of whether these patterns identified here represent idiosyncratic features of my corpus or structural characteristics of aesthetic discourse in general.
Art Movement Manifestos: Do avant-garde manifestos reveal structural patterns behind explicit programs?
Cross-Cultural Comparison: Does the language-aesthetics dialectic operate similarly across linguistic and cultural contexts?
Digital Discourse Analysis: How does the dialectic operate within algorithmically mediated environments?

More fundamentally, future work should apply computational auto-archaeology to texts where the analyst is not the author. This would remove the "auto-" dimension but retain the method. Could the same procedure discern unconscious patterns in how Rancière theorized aesthetics and politics? In Foucault's analysis of discourse and power? Applications like these would make auto-archaeology a general method for aesthetic philosophy, revealing the conceptual architectures organizing aesthetic theory itself and not just one philosopher's contribution to it.

div.head: 7. Conclusion: Toward an Empirically Grounded Aesthetic Theory
div.p: The computational turn need not mean positivist reduction. Digital analysis provides discourse-level evidence for theory, offering patterns consistent with Rancière's political aesthetics while acknowledging that such patterns may reflect theoretical influence rather than independent confirmation.

The methodological contribution is equally significant. Computational auto-archaeology shows that digital humanities methods can serve aesthetic philosophy, not by replacing interpretation but by identifying patterns that interpretation must address. It offers what the original short note termed an "aesthetic of self-reflection," a means of mapping the dialectic that organizes discourse (Mastroianni, 2025). This reflexive dimension — the philosopher analyzing their own conceptual development — contributes to an empirical-interpretive practice, connecting theoretical claims to discourse patterns revealed through systematic analysis.

The philosopher who would develop an adequate aesthetic theory must employ methods that reveal how aesthetics operates — not just consciously in explicit arguments, but structurally in discourse patterns; not just individually in particular artworks, but systematically in the distribution of the sensible. Computational auto-archaeology provides one such methodology, contributing to a more empirically rigorous, interpretively nuanced, and politically relevant aesthetic theory.

As digital technologies mediate aesthetic experience and algorithms shape perception, this theory becomes urgent. Understanding power's preconscious aesthetic operations may enable resistance to develop effective counter-strategies and generate new distributions of the sensible.

The computational turn in aesthetic philosophy, properly understood, is not a turn away from philosophy toward data science, but a turn toward new methods for revealing the structures organizing thought. This article demonstrates one such method, showing how computational analysis can identify patterns within conceptual architectures in philosophical discourse. The patterns revealed — the dialectic between language and aesthetics, between conscious critique and preconscious experience — suggest new possibilities for aesthetic theory in the twenty-first century.
